title: Is it a restroom or a loo?

entries.note: The most common US word for a police officer; in Britain it mostly appears in tabloid headlines because it is shorter than police.
Common in London; it may come from the verb to cop, to catch, or from the copper badges of the NYPD, which may be folk etymology.
The most common use of cop as a verb in the US, and not a polite thing to do; related to [[see:copper]].
US underworld slang for police; it may come from force, from fuss (meaning over-particular), or from buzz-cut police haircuts.
A British police comedy film the hosts love; it made them think [[see:fuzz]] was British.
US hobo slang for police; railroad bulls guarded trains against robbers and people riding illegally.
Used on both sides of the Atlantic; in London slang a pig was an informant or plain-clothes officer, and it was kept alive by cartoon portrayals of police.
Compared with [[see:pigs]] as a word for a duplicitous person or informant.
A word for police, for the same reason as [[see:pigs]]; a friend from Essex used to say 'oink oink, I smell bacon'.
An English word for police, from [[from:Robert Peel]], who set up the Metropolitan Police when he was Home Secretary.
Former British prime minister who set up the Metropolitan Police, the Royal Irish Constabulary and the Conservative Party; source of [[gave:Bobby]] and [[gave:peelers]].
A word for police in Ireland, especially Northern Ireland, after [[from:Robert Peel]].
US slang from the 1960s to the 1980s for a bumbling police officer, after [[from:Barney Fife]].
The inept officer played by Don Knotts on [[see:The Andy Griffith Show]], who gave us [[gave:Barney]].
The US TV show that featured [[see:Barney Fife]].
Cockney rhyming slang from Barney Rubble, rhyming with trouble; the hosts note it must be modern because it uses an American TV character.
Highway patrol police, as in [[see:Smokey and the Bandit]], named after [[from:Smokey Bear]] because of their similar hats.
A film in which the highway patrol cops are called [[see:Smokies]].
Highway patrol officers were nicknamed [[gave:Smokies]] after him because they wear a similar hat.
Police on patrol, especially in big US cities; the British talk of Bobbies on the beat.
Patrolling police, perhaps because walking flattens their feet or because they are bumbling and clumsy.
Slang for police actively chasing suspects, from the idea that the heat is on.
Slang for police from the 1960s show [[from:Hawaii Five-O]].
A nickname for police, similar to war nicknames like [[see:Tommies]], [[see:Charlie]] and [[see:Billy Yank]].
A war nickname compared with [[see:Johnny Law]].
A war nickname compared with [[see:Johnny Law]].
A war nickname compared with [[see:Johnny Law]].
A slang word for police whose origin the hosts call pretty obvious.
In Jamaican reggae culture, any corrupt and oppressive authority, including the police, because Babylon is associated with corruption.
US slang for federal agencies like the FBI and DEA; in Britain, which has no federal police, it is only used ironically or pretentiously.
One of the American terms for different kinds of police.
American slang for private detectives.
From a French word for a deputy, someone you turn to; it became a dirty word in Britain, which Samuel Johnson mocked.
British word for a lawyer who gives legal advice; from [[from:solicit]], whose origin means to provoke, disturb or agitate.
British lawyer who specialises in representing clients once a case gets to court; used partly because [[see:attorney]] had become a dirty word.
The only British attorney Rob can think of: the Crown's chief legal adviser.
King's Counsel, formerly QC (Queen's Counsel): a high-ranking [[see:barrister]] recognised for excellence in advocacy.
A general term for all of these; in the US a lawyer has finished law school, while an [[see:attorney]] has also passed the bar.
Contrasted with an [[see:attorney]], who represents you.
To encourage an action, as in sex work or selling; 'no soliciting' signs ban salespeople, not lawyers; it gave [[gave:solicitor]].
Can also mean an advertisement in a public space; related to [[same-root:solicit]].
Abbreviation of versus, written without a dot in Britain and with one in the US; legal cases use v. as in [[see:Roe v. Wade]].
A landmark legal case that shows the American v. abbreviation of [[see:vs]].
British for a pharmacy; from [[from:alchemist]], whose al- was mistaken for the Arabic definite article and dropped, as with [[see:chemistry]].
Also lost the al- of alchemy, like [[see:chemist]].
The more common word for a shop selling medicine; from a Greek word that could mean poison or even witchcraft.
Affected by metathesis, so some people say 'perscription'.
A short US word for prescriptions.
Used on both sides of the Atlantic for medicine that needs no prescription.
Rob calls this an Americanism that Britons wouldn't use.
The American word for a pharmacy, which Rob teasingly calls moronic.
In the US, a place selling legal medical or recreational cannabis, unlike a [[see:drugstore]].
Archaic in English; from Latin [[from:apotheca]], storehouse, the root of [[same-root:boutique]] and [[same-root:bodega]]; probably dropped because it became tied to dubious 1800s drugs.
The everyday German word for a pharmacy, which recalls the archaic English [[same-root:apothecary]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:apothecary]], Latin [[from:apotheca]], storehouse.
Shares a root with [[same-root:apothecary]], Latin [[from:apotheca]], showing a P–B swap.
A remedy made of alcohol, sassafras, clove and camphor and sold in America until the 1920s; an example of dubious [[see:apothecary]] medicine.
Literally means dry, from dry goods; fits a G/Y swap like [[see:day]] and [[see:way]]; has meant poison since the 1500s.
An Old English word that had a G at the end, an example of the G/Y swap seen in [[see:drug]].
Another example of the G/Y swap mentioned with [[see:drug]].
The usual British word for a major road; Americans say [[see:highway]] or [[see:interstate]].
Dates from Old English, where high meant main, the main way between towns; Britain uses it in the [[see:Highway Code]].
The British book of road rules, which shows Britain does recognise the idea of a [[see:highway]].
First meant the trading of slaves between southern states, then interstate commerce; only after the [[see:Eisenhower Interstate System]] did it mean a road.
Road network built to move the military quickly; Jess blames it for car dependence and the lack of high-speed rail.
Not a road with two lanes: two carriageways (strips of tarmac) carry traffic in opposite directions, separated by a barrier.
British for road surfacing; in the US the word is used only at airports.
The US word for the road surface material that Britons call [[see:tarmac]].
In Britain, the walkway beside the road; in the US it is just a surface material, like [[see:asphalt]].
The US word for what Britons call the [[see:pavement]].
Only certain US roads, like the New Jersey Turnpike, are called this; in Britain the toll-collecting Turnpike Trusts are gone and the word has slipped out of use.
A road, originally broken-up ground like that dug with a pike; perhaps also influenced by [[see?:pitch]], the tar.
Tar put down on roads, which may have influenced [[see?:pike]].
British roads that are [[see:motorway]]s.
British roads that are [[see:dual carriageway]]s.
British roads that are slightly smaller than [[see:A roads]].
Technically the smallest British road class, which people rarely talk about.
Rob always uses this word, though others call them [[see:traffic circles]] or [[see:traffic islands]].
Another name for a [[see:roundabout]].
Another name for a [[see:roundabout]].
German for exit; Jess's American family joked about where 'Fart, Germany' was; compare [[see:Einfahrt]].
German for entrance, the counterpart of [[see:Ausfahrt]].
The British word for fuel; Americans say [[see:gas]].
The US word for car fuel, though it is liquid; it makes sense as a shortening of [[from:gasoline]].
From [[from:Cazeline]], named by [[see:John Cassell]]; [[see:John Boyd]] respelled his counterfeit, and US refiners reinterpreted it as gas + oleum + -ine.
John Cassell's name for his refined lamp oil, with a Greek suffix meaning olive: Cassell oil; it led to [[gave:gasoline]].
Englishman who sold refined petroleum for lamps and named it [[see:Cazeline]] after himself.
Irishman who sold counterfeit [[see:Cazeline]] and changed the spelling after Cassell objected, producing [[gave:gasoline]].
Contains the same Latin oleum, oil, that refiners read into [[see:gasoline]].
Used on both sides of the Atlantic; named after [[from:Rudolf Diesel]], the German inventor of an internal combustion engine.
British for the car's rear storage, perhaps from the coachman's boot, a storage box on carriages; the hosts can't fully explain it.
The American word for a car's [[see:boot]].
British for the front cover of a car; logically the same idea as [[see:hood]].
The American word for a car's [[see:bonnet]].
British word; it seems odd to Jess, since to her a [[see:screen]] is wire mesh.
The US word for a [[see:windscreen]], which Rob admits makes more sense.
Discussed in an earlier episode; it means both to block and to enable viewing, which explains [[see:windscreen]].
The British word for a car's [[see:turn signals]].
The US word for [[see:indicators]].
An old British portmanteau of traffic and [[from:indicators]], still used in Nigerian English.
In South African English, a traffic light.
Rob's word, never [[see:intersection]]; in the US it is usually part of a street name.
Never used by Rob, who says [[see:junction]].
Britons sometimes say 'a couple of blocks over', which makes little sense in Britain's spiderweb streets, outside grid towns like Milton Keynes.
The US form; Americans never say [[see:aeroplane]], though they do say aerospace.
The British form of [[see:airplane]].
Branded in the US and so more common there than [[see:zip]]; one of the few transatlantic differences in a modern invention's name.
The British word for a [[see:zipper]].
Used by both hosts for a trouser opening; they don't know why and ask viewers to explain.
May come from French [[from?:lieu d'aisance]], place of ease, or a joke on [[see?:Waterloo]]; recorded early in [[see:Ulysses]], and common only from the 1920s.
The supposed basis of a [[see?:loo]] joke about water closets, which the hosts doubt on chronological grounds.
James Joyce's novel, which contains one of the first recorded colloquial uses of [[see:loo]].
Rarely used in Britain, though WC appears on signs.
Itself a euphemism, from a French word for a towel.
Originally a separate room for resting and relaxing in public buildings or workplaces, a precursor to the break room.
Originally a room with a bath, usually larger and public; now a euphemism for where you wash your hands.
Another euphemism, a room where you wash your hands.
Standard in Jess's house but not in the US; the hosts pronounce it differently, and Rob played with the fountain in his childhood one.
A brand name from [[see:3M]], from scotch as a slur meaning cheap, because early tape had adhesive only on the edges.
Formerly Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing, maker of [[see:Scotch tape]], which it now sells with tartan inside the roll.
One of only two acceptable uses of scotch, unlike [[see:Scotch tape]].
The other acceptable use of scotch, unlike [[see:Scotch tape]].
The British word for clear tape, a portmanteau of cellophane and tape.
Another British word for [[see:Scotch tape]].
A Harry Potter joke on [[see:Sellotape]], which Jess didn't get as a child; publishers didn't need to change it for Americans.

entries.term: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
entries.note: The first Harry Potter book's title was changed for Americans, a transatlantic difference the hosts have covered before.
Used to dry dishes after tea; also used in the US for a cuter decorative towel, distinct from a [[see:dish towel]]; the subject of Rob's dad's owl pun.
In Jess's family, the plainer towel used for drying dishes, distinct from a [[see:tea towel]].
An American alternative name for a [[see:tea towel]].
In Jess's family, a different thing from a [[see:tea towel]] and a [[see:dish towel]].
An older British name for a [[see:tea towel]], still sometimes heard.
The British word for the cooking top of an oven, which Americans call a [[see:stove]].
Also a freestanding heater; slightly old-fashioned in Britain; from Old English [[from:stofa]], a steam or sweating room.
From Ottoman Turkish sofa, a raised ledge for resting on; the word manufacturers use.
Jess's word; via Old French couche, a place to lie down, from the Latin root of [[same-root:collocate]], to place together; Rob would think it Americanised.
Jess's Victorian-style grandmother had one, more like an upholstered bench or fainting couch.
From the same Latin root as [[same-root:couch]], meaning to place together.
The French word for a nappy, a relative of [[same-root:couch]].
Originally a patterned white cloth; from French, meaning thoroughly white, from Greek; used by Shakespeare; Jess dislikes the word.
Short for baby's napkin, and probably younger than [[see:diaper]].
From a term for a white cloth, because Roman candidates for office often wore bright white; compared with [[see:diaper]].
Used on both sides; Jess also says [[see:drapes]], perhaps because her mother sews them.
A US word for [[see:curtains]] that Jess uses.
